nameStory: Pediastrum gets its name from the Greek words 'pedion' meaning 'flat surface' and 'astron' meaning 'star,' referring to how these tiny algae arrange themselves in flat, star-like colonies that look like green wheels floating in water. The species name 'obtusum' means 'blunt' in Latin, describing the rounded, blunt edges of the outer cells in each colony. While it doesn't have a widely-used common name, some scientists call it the 'blunt wheel alga' for its distinctive shape.
description: Pediastrum obtusum is a microscopic freshwater green alga that forms flat, circular colonies resembling tiny green wheels or pizza slices floating in pond water. Each colony is made up of 4-32 individual cells arranged in a single flat layer, with the whole colony measuring only about 0.1-0.3 millimeters across—so small you'd need a magnifying glass or microscope to see the beautiful geometric patterns clearly. These colonies drift freely in the water column of ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. While invisible to the naked eye individually, they can sometimes contribute to the greenish tinge you might notice in nutrient-rich water bodies.

idTips.label: Colony shape
idTips.description: Forms perfectly flat, circular colonies that look like tiny green wheels with cells arranged like puzzle pieces—no raised bumps or three-dimensional structure

idTips.label: Outer cell shape
idTips.description: The cells around the edge of each colony have distinctly blunt, rounded outer margins rather than pointed projections or horns

idTips.label: Cell arrangement
idTips.description: Individual cells fit together tightly like pieces of a jigsaw puzzle with no gaps between them, creating a solid disk

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Colonies contain anywhere from 4 to 32 cells, with larger colonies showing more complex geometric patterns

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright green color typical of chlorophyll-rich algae, often appearing as a greenish tint in the water

habitat: Found floating freely in the water of nutrient-rich ponds, small lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England's lowlands. It thrives in water bodies with moderate to high nutrient levels, often where there's some organic matter from fallen leaves or agricultural runoff. You're most likely to encounter it in shallow, sun-warmed waters where other green algae and aquatic plants are also abundant.

seasonality.spring: Colonies begin forming as water temperatures rise and daylight increases, often becoming noticeable in late spring when pond water starts showing a greenish tint.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when colonies reproduce rapidly, sometimes contributing to algal blooms in nutrient-rich waters.
seasonality.fall: Populations typically decline as temperatures drop and daylight decreases, though some colonies may persist in protected, sun-warmed shallows.
seasonality.winter: Largely dormant or absent from the water column, surviving harsh conditions as specialized resting cells that will germinate when favorable conditions return.

funFact: Each Pediastrum colony starts as a single cell that divides internally to produce all its offspring, which then arrange themselves into the perfect geometric pattern before breaking out of the parent cell wall—like nature's own 3D printer creating living mandalas!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its relatives Pediastrum duplex (which has distinctive horn-like projections on outer cells) and Pediastrum angulosum (which has angular, pointed outer cells). Remember: obtusum = obtuse angles = blunt and rounded edges, while the others are pointy.
contextualKnowledge: Though called an 'alga,' Pediastrum is actually more closely related to land plants than to seaweeds, representing an ancient lineage that hints at how plant life first colonized freshwater environments millions of years ago.
compareHints: Unlike Pediastrum duplex with its characteristic horn-like projections on outer cells, P. obtusum has smoothly rounded outer margins. It also differs from Pediastrum angulosum, which has distinctly angular, pointed outer cells that give colonies a more star-like appearance. The blunt, rounded edges are the key feature that sets obtusum apart from its spiky relatives.
